title: POC scoping - Benchmark harness integration (streaming vs non-streaming)
header:
Date: 2026-08-21
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 mins
Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE); Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE); Diego Rivera (Redwood CSM); Jordan Lee (DataHarbor - Head of ML); Samir Patel (DataHarbor - Infra Lead); Maya Chen (DataHarbor - PM); Evan Cho (DataHarbor - SRE)
summary: POC scoping call to align success criteria, workload sizing, and how to integrate DataHarbor's benchmark scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness. Discussed streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, load profiles, tooling (k6/locust/custom scripts), and a 2-3 week POC timeline with initial benchmarking run on reserved capacity.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna quickly run through scope for the benchmark harness integration for the POC. um, quick roll call?
[00:08] Jordan: Jordan here, hey.
[00:10] Samir: Samir on infra.
[00:12] Maya: Maya, product.
[00:14] Evan: Evan, SRE.
[00:16] Priya: Priya from Redwood, hi all.
[00:18] Alex: Great. so objective for today is to capture success criteria, the expected load patterns, and what scripts you have so Priya can map to our harness, right.
[00:30] Jordan: Yeah, we want to validate that latency p95 for short chat gen flows is under 300ms for the hosted option, and for Dedicated we'd like under 200 at p95. Cost per 1k tokens is also important, we have internal budget targets.
[00:48] Priya: ok, when you say short chat gen flows, what's the token length distribution?
[00:54] Jordan: Mostly prompts are 30-80 tokens, responses 40-150, average around 120 tokens per request. but there are longer occasional batch jobs ~1k tokens.
[01:10] Samir: traffic wise, we're expecting spikes during product launches: baseline 20 rps, peak 200 rps for 10-15 minutes, sustained 60 rps during business hours. Concurrency around 500 active sessions.
[01:28] Alex: that's helpful. For the benchmark we usually run a few profiles: steady-state, spike tests, and soak. We'll want a steady at 60 rps for 30 minutes, a spike to 200 rps for 15 minutes, and a 24-hour soak for cost extrapolation — we can shorten the soak for POC.
[01:47] Maya: For success criteria, aside from latency/cost we need correctness/regression checks vs current model responses — so we need to run a sample eval set.
[01:58] Priya: yes, we can wire in your eval set. do you have deterministic prompts or do they have dynamic context?
[02:06] Jordan: A mix. Most are deterministic; some include user history. we'll provide a sample corpus with ~1k prompts and about 200 multi-turn sessions.
[02:18] Evan: infra question — will you be provisioning Dedicated for the benchmark or are we running against hosted first?
[02:24] Alex: We recommend starting hosted to validate integration, then run the Dedicated profile if you want to test isolation and autoscaling. For Dedicated we can reserve a small pool for the POC.
[02:36] Samir: ok, important to test KV cache behavior for multi-turn. Does Redwood's harness simulate warm KV cache?
[02:44] Priya: yes, we have a warm-up phase that can pre-populate KV cache with your session prefixes so the benchmark can reflect steady-state latency. we'll document the warm-up steps.
[02:53] Jordan: cool. about the harness itself, we currently have k6 scripts and a small node.js harness that talks to our front end. is k6 supported?
[03:03] Priya: absolutely, k6 and locust are both supported, plus we can run customer scripts inside a docker runner. For streaming vs non-streaming, k6 is typically non-streaming, so if you need to test streaming responses we recommend our custom harness or a headless chrome approach for the frontend.
[03:22] Alex: quick note: streaming changes how throughput and connection counts behave — long-lived connections vs many short requests. that impacts autoscaler settings and LB timeouts.
[03:33] Evan: yeah we need to measure connection churn. during streaming flows we maintain websocket/chunked responses and that reduces rps but increases concurrent connections.
[03:43] Priya: we'll add a streaming profile: X concurrent streaming sessions for Y minutes, and measure p95 time-to-first-token and end-to-end completion time. Also we'll capture connection counts and file descriptors.
[03:56] Samir: also want to track tail latency p99 and error rates under spike.
[04:02] Priya: noted. we'll instrument with trace IDs and provide logs and trace links.
[04:08] Jordan: For the harness integration, the steps we expect: provide scripts -> Redwood maps into harness -> run smoke -> run full benches -> share results + config for tuning. approximate timeline?
[04:20] Alex: for an initial run: provide scripts and corpus by Monday, we map and do a smoke in 2-3 days, full run within a week. Dedicated run might take extra time to provision, say another week. so overall 2-3 weeks for a full POC.
[04:34] Maya: ok that aligns. Data residency & logs question: logs and traces from the harness — are those stored in Redwood console?
[04:42] Diego: Diego here — we store run artifacts in the customer's project in the console; for private deployments we can route logs to your SIEM, and for hosted we'd keep them for the agreed retention period.
[04:51] Evan: encryption — we'll need KMS integration for any test data on Dedicated or Private.
[04:57] Priya: we can support customer KMS for Dedicated and Private. for hosted we'd need to confirm the contract/controls.
[05:05] Jordan: on tooling, we use k6 for throughput tests and a small puppeteer script for streaming UX tests. can we run both in the same harness run?
[05:12] Priya: yes, we can orchestrate multiple runners. we'll coordinate the sequence so warm-up happens before streaming tests.
[05:20] Samir: load generator placement question: should we run k6 from Redwood infra or from our VPC?
[05:26] Alex: either works; running from Redwood's cloud simplifies latency-to-model measurements (less cross-VPC noise). running from your VPC can simulate customer network conditions — we recommend doing both for thoroughness.
[05:38] Jordan: about metrics — we want token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency, and per-model throughput.
[05:45] Priya: all available. we'll export a benchmark report with token counts, cost estimates using current price table, and recommendations (batching, quantization, model variant).
[05:55] Maya: do you support quantized models during POC? we want to see perf/cost delta between fp16 and 4-bit.
[06:02] Priya: yes, we can test quantized variants, but for correctness evaluation we should run the eval set against both variants to compare regressions.
[06:12] Jordan: another ask: can we test a fallback policy? e.g., when Dedicated is saturated, fall back to a smaller model or hosted. we need to ensure graceful degradation.
[06:21] Alex: absolutely. we can script a cascade policy and include a failure injection phase in the spike test to validate fallbacks.
[06:29] Evan: are there rate-limit artifacts or client SDK changes needed for streaming? our frontend uses an SDK that expects stream tokens; if we do non-streamed bursts maybe it will break UX.
[06:40] Priya: we'll share SDK compatibility notes; usually streaming vs non-stream differences are limited to connection handling and event parsing.
[06:48] Samir: about observability, we want traces to align with our existing tracing. can Redwood emit traceparent headers?
[06:55] Diego: yes we support distributed tracing headers and can correlate with your traces.
[07:00] Jordan: perfect. on reporting cadence, we want raw results + a summary deck + the run scripts.
[07:08] Alex: we'll provide those artifacts and a follow-up meeting to review results.
[07:12] Maya: timeline recap?
[07:14] Alex: customer provides scripts and eval set by 2026-08-24, Redwood maps to harness by 2026-08-26, smoke run 08-27, full runs complete by 09-03, Dedicated validation by 09-10 (if requested).
[07:29] Jordan: sounds good.
[07:31] Priya: quick technical note on streaming vs non-streaming — when you stream, CPU overhead per token is lower in some runtimes due to early return, but connection memory stays higher. non-streamed requests can achieve higher RPS because connections are short lived; however p95 per-request may be a bit higher if batching is aggressive.
[07:53] Samir: ok we need the exact configs you'll use — batch sizes, KV cache window, tokenization settings.
[08:00] Priya: we'll include a conf file per run. example: batch target 16, max sequence 512, prefill cache size 100 sessions, quantization flags.
[08:10] Evan: we'll also want disk/network util metrics on the inference nodes during runs.
[08:15] Priya: we can export host metrics and GPU utilization heatmaps.
[08:19] Jordan: any gotchas?
[08:22] Alex: two common ones: 1) not warming KV cache before measuring steady-state 2) comparing streaming p95 to non-streaming p95 directly without considering time-to-first-token vs end-to-end. avoid both.
[08:36] Maya: ok, next steps and action owners?
[08:39] Alex: yep we'll capture those.
[08:42] Jordan: thanks all.
[08:44] (call winds down, small cross talk)

Redwood to map scripts into benchmark harness and share runbook by 2026-08-26
